script.title: Year-end tax moves for freelancers (and the ones to skip)
script.hook: December is when freelancers get the worst tax advice of the year: buy a car, buy a laptop, write everything off. Some year-end moves really do lower your bill. Most of the popular ones just move money from you to a store. Here's how to tell the difference, with twenty twenty-six numbers. Education, not tax advice. We'll start with where you stand, then six moves worth considering and the ones to skip.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: December is when freelancers get the worst tax advice of the year: buy a car, buy a laptop, write everything off. Some year-end moves really do lower your bill. Most of the popular ones just move money from you to a store. Here's how to tell the difference, with twenty twenty-six numbers. Education, not tax advice. We'll start with where you stand, then six moves worth considering and the ones to skip.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes under a December calendar holding a short checklist. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Where you stand
segments.narration: Before any move, know where you stand. Take your profit so far this year, add what you realistically expect to collect in December, and work out the full-year tax with our calculator or your tracker. Then compare it with what you've paid in estimates and what's in your tax savings account. That one number, how much you'll still owe, decides which of the moves below are worth your time. If you're already short, the best year-end move is simply saving more before January fifteenth.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes studying a gauge on a coral vault. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Write-off math
segments.narration: First, the math everyone skips. A business deduction lowers your profit, which lowers both self-employment tax and income tax. At sixty thousand of profit, a single filer saves about two hundred thirty dollars per thousand dollars of deductions. At a hundred and twenty thousand, about three hundred five. So a deduction saves you a quarter to a third of the cost. You still pay the rest.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a big coin next to a small coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Timing
segments.narration: That's why the real year-end move is timing, not spending. If you were going to buy a laptop in February anyway, buying it and starting to use it in December moves the deduction a year earlier. If you weren't going to buy it, don't. The same goes for supplies, upgrades and repairs. Make a short list of what the business genuinely needs in the next two or three months, check the cash in your business account after setting aside tax, and only then decide what to buy now.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a box moving from February to December. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Equipment rules
segments.narration: If you are buying equipment, three rules. It has to be placed in service, meaning set up and used for the business, by December thirty-first. Buying it on the thirtieth and leaving it in the box doesn't count. You deduct only the business share, so a laptop used seventy percent for work is a seventy percent deduction. And small items, generally up to twenty-five hundred dollars each, can usually be written off right away as supplies if you follow that election. Bigger items can usually be written off in year one too, but keep the receipt and note how you use it.
segments.on_screen_text: In service by Dec 31 · business % only
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a laptop on a desk, switched on, with a calendar showing Dec 31. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Invoices
segments.narration: Second, invoice timing. Most freelancers use the cash method: income counts when you receive it. A payment that arrives January second is next year's income. Don't play games with clients' payment dates, but don't rush to collect a December invoice if it suits you to receive it in January either.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an invoice crossing into January. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Pay bills
segments.narration: A related timing move on the expense side: bills. On the cash method, an expense counts when you pay it. Charges on a credit card count when you make the charge, not when you pay the card. So paying your January software renewal or your accountant's invoice on December twenty-ninth moves the deduction into this year. Again, only for things you'd pay anyway. And don't prepay a year or more in advance just for the deduction; the rules generally limit prepaid expenses to benefits that don't extend beyond twelve months.
segments.on_screen_text: Expenses count when paid (card = when charged)
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar page with a coin moving from January to December. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Retirement
segments.narration: Third, retirement. A SEP IRA can be opened and funded until your filing deadline, including extensions, and still count for this year. That's roughly twenty percent of profit after half of self-employment tax. A Solo 401(k) allows more, but its setup and election deadlines are stricter, so ask your provider before December thirty-first. An IRA works too, seventy-five hundred dollars for twenty twenty-six, until April fifteenth.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three plant pots. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Estimate
segments.narration: Fourth, update your estimate. Take your profit so far, add what you expect in December, and work out the full-year bill. That tells you how big the January fifteenth payment needs to be, and whether your tax savings will cover the April balance. If the January number looks scary, remember you can make extra payments any time before then, and anything you pay now is money you won't need to find in April. Even a partial top-up helps.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calculator and a January page. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Jan 15 math
segments.narration: Here's a quick example of sizing that January payment. Say last year's total tax was sixty-five hundred dollars and you've paid sixteen twenty-five in April, June and September. Under the safe harbor, January is another sixteen twenty-five, and you're generally protected from the penalty. But if this year's real tax is about twelve thousand, you'll still owe about fifty-five hundred more in April. So the safe harbor protects you from the penalty, not from the bill. Your tax savings account needs to cover both.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four coin stacks and a larger one waiting in April. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Health
segments.narration: Fifth, health insurance. If you buy your own, pick next year's plan on the marketplace by December fifteenth for coverage from January first. Bronze and catastrophic plans now count as HSA-compatible, and self-employed premiums are often deductible.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a medical shield and a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Big year or small
segments.narration: Here's the thinking behind all this timing. If you expect a bigger income next year, deductions are worth more next year and income is taxed more next year, so you'd rather pull income into this year and push deductions out. If this was your big year, do the opposite: pull deductions in and let late payments land in January. Most freelancers don't know which way next year will go, and that's fine. When in doubt, don't contort anything; just make sure nothing you need slips through the cracks.
segments.on_screen_text: Big year now? Pull deductions in
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a seesaw tilting between two calendar pages. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Paperwork
segments.narration: Sixth, paperwork. If you paid another freelancer two thousand dollars or more directly this year, ask for their W-9 now so you can send a 1099-NEC by February first. And catch up your income and expense logs while December is quiet.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a stack of forms and a ledger. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Next year
segments.narration: And use the quiet week between Christmas and New Year to set up next year. A separate tax savings account if you don't have one. A set-aside percentage based on this year's real numbers. New logs for income, expenses and miles. And a photo of your car's odometer on December thirty-first, because your mileage log starts with that number. Twenty minutes of setup now saves you a weekend next January.
segments.on_screen_text: Set up next year in 20 minutes
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes placing a new notebook next to three jars. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: And one unglamorous move that pays off more than any purchase: get your records straight before the year closes. Go through November and December's business bank and card statements. Label anything unclear while you still remember what it was. Make sure every business expense paid from a personal card is logged. Add up your miles. When January comes, you'll be able to size the last payment in ten minutes and start your return with real numbers instead of guesses.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes labeling lines on a long bank statement. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Charity
segments.narration: A quick note on charity, because December is when people ask. Donations from your business aren't business expenses for a sole proprietor; they're personal charitable contributions. Under the newer rules, people who take the standard deduction can deduct a limited amount of cash gifts starting in twenty twenty-six, so check the current limit. If you itemize, they work as before. Give because you care about the cause, and keep the receipt either way.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small heart dropping into a jar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Skip
segments.narration: Now the ones to skip. Buying a vehicle you don't need for the deduction. Prepaying next year's subscriptions just to pull the deduction forward, which often isn't allowed beyond twelve months anyway. And anything a stranger online calls a loophole. If you couldn't explain it calmly to an auditor, don't do it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shopping cart with a small stop sign. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: time purchases you needed anyway, know when income counts, fund retirement, size the January payment, sort health insurance, and collect W-9s. The free calculator in the description does the January math. Pick the two or three that apply to you this week, put them on your calendar, and ignore the rest. script.title: LLC, S corp or sole proprietor? What actually changes
script.hook: Every new freelancer gets told to form an LLC, and every freelancer earning decent money gets told to become an S corp. Both can be right. Both are often wrong. Here's what each one actually changes, so you can decide on purpose. Education only; state rules vary. We'll cover the myths, liability and insurance, real S corp numbers, the reasonable salary rule, side effects, and the order to do things in if you decide to switch.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Every new freelancer gets told to form an LLC, and every freelancer earning decent money gets told to become an S corp. Both can be right. Both are often wrong. Here's what each one actually changes, so you can decide on purpose. Education only; state rules vary. We'll cover the myths, liability and insurance, real S corp numbers, the reasonable salary rule, side effects, and the order to do things in if you decide to switch.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes standing before three simple buildings. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Sole prop
segments.narration: The default is the sole proprietorship. You start one the moment you take paid work under your own name. No filing needed. You report profit on Schedule C and pay self-employment tax. Your business and personal assets aren't legally separate. For most new freelancers, that's perfectly fine.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a single small building. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Myths
segments.narration: Let's clear up three myths before going further. Myth one: an LLC lets you deduct more. It doesn't; the same expenses are deductible as a sole proprietor. Myth two: an LLC means you don't pay self-employment tax. By default you pay exactly the same. Myth three: you need an LLC to look professional or to open a business bank account. Many banks open business accounts for sole proprietors, and clients care about your work, your contract and your invoices, not your entity.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small speech bubbles crossed out. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: LLC taxes
segments.narration: An LLC is a state legal entity. For federal tax, a single-member LLC is ignored by default. Same Schedule C, same self-employment tax, same deductions. So an LLC by itself doesn't save tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two identical forms. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: LLC liability
segments.narration: What an LLC can do is limit your personal liability for business debts and some claims, as long as you keep the money separate and follow your state's rules. It won't protect you from your own professional mistakes. That's what professional liability insurance is for.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a wall between a briefcase and a house. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Insurance
segments.narration: Since we're talking about protection: for most solo freelancers, the real risk isn't business debt, it's a client claiming your work caused them a loss. That's what professional liability insurance, sometimes called errors and omissions, is for. And if clients visit you or you work on their premises, general liability covers injuries and damage. An LLC can't do either of those jobs. For a lot of freelancers, a decent insurance policy is a better first step than forming an entity.
segments.on_screen_text: Insurance does what an LLC can't
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a shield with a small umbrella. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Separate
segments.narration: If you do form an LLC, the protection only holds up if you treat it as separate. That means a separate bank account, contracts signed in the LLC's name, and not paying personal bills from the business account. Mixing money is the classic way people lose the liability shield in court. It's also how they lose track of deductions. The good news is that separate accounts are a good idea whether you form an LLC or not.
segments.on_screen_text: Keep it separate or lose the shield
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two jars with a clear wall between them. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: LLC cost
segments.narration: LLCs cost money. Every state charges a filing fee, many require an annual report, and some charge an annual fee or tax. California's minimum is eight hundred dollars a year. Check your state before you form one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin dropping into a state outline. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: S corp
segments.narration: An S corp is a tax election, available to an LLC or a corporation. You pay yourself a reasonable salary through payroll, with Social Security and Medicare taxes withheld. Profit above that salary isn't subject to self-employment tax. That's the saving.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack split in two. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Numbers
segments.narration: Let's put rough numbers on the S corp. Say your profit is a hundred thousand dollars. As a sole proprietor, self-employment tax is about fourteen thousand one hundred. As an S corp paying yourself a sixty thousand dollar salary, payroll taxes on that salary are about nine thousand two hundred, employer and employee halves together. That's roughly five thousand dollars of difference before costs. Then subtract payroll software, the extra business return, state fees and a bookkeeper or accountant, which can easily be two to four thousand a year. And the income tax side shifts a little too. So the real saving here might be one to three thousand, not the ten thousand people promise online.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two coin stacks with a few coins removed from one for fees. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Reasonable
segments.narration: That salary is the part people get wrong. The IRS expects an S corp owner who works in the business to pay themselves reasonable compensation: roughly what you'd pay someone else to do your job. You can't pay yourself ten thousand dollars and take ninety thousand as distributions. Look at what employees in your field and area earn, document how you chose the number, and expect a CPA to push back if it's low. The lower the salary, the bigger the saving looks, and the bigger the risk.
segments.on_screen_text: Salary = what you'd pay someone else
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a balance scale with a paycheck on one side. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: S corp cost
segments.narration: The costs: payroll software, a separate business tax return, usually an accountant, sometimes state taxes, and the salary must be reasonable for your work. The saving only beats the cost once profit is well above that salary. Run the numbers with a CPA before electing, and plan for the extra paperwork.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three receipts in a row. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Side effects
segments.narration: There are side effects worth knowing. Your retirement contributions as an S corp are based on your salary, not your whole profit, so a low salary can limit them. The qualified business income deduction is figured differently. Health insurance has to go through payroll to be deductible for an owner. And you'll be filing payroll reports every quarter. None of that is a deal-breaker, but each one is a reason to run the numbers with a professional who sees your whole picture.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. four small icons on a checklist. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Multi-member
segments.narration: One more structure to know about: if you go into business with a partner, things change. A multi-member LLC is taxed as a partnership by default, which means a separate partnership return and a Schedule K-1 for each owner. Each partner still pays self-employment tax on their share. Partnerships need a written agreement covering who owns what, how profits are split and what happens if someone leaves. If you're thinking of teaming up, get that agreement in place before the money starts coming in.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two small mascots holding one shared folder. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: When
segments.narration: A simple rule of thumb: start as a sole proprietor with a separate business account and good records. Add an LLC when you have something to protect or a client requires it. Consider an S corp when your profit is high and steady and a CPA shows the saving after costs.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small plant growing taller in stages. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: How to switch
segments.narration: If you decide to switch, the order is usually: form the LLC with your state, get a free EIN from the IRS, open a business bank account in the LLC's name, and update your contracts and W-9s. For an S corp, file Form twenty-five fifty-three. To have it apply from the start of a calendar year, it's generally due by March fifteenth of that year. You can change structure as your business grows, so you don't need to get this perfect on day one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a short path with four stepping stones. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Decide
segments.narration: So how do you actually decide? Ask three questions. First: what could go wrong that would cost me personally, and would an LLC or insurance address it? Second: is my profit high and steady enough that an S corp saves money after all its costs, according to someone who has seen my numbers? Third: am I ready for the extra paperwork? If the answers are not really, not yet and no, stay a sole proprietor with separate accounts and good records, and revisit next year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a checklist with three question marks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mistakes
segments.narration: And the three most expensive mistakes we see. Forming an S corp at forty thousand of profit, where the costs eat the saving. Forming an LLC in another state, like Delaware or Wyoming, when you live and work somewhere else, and then paying fees in both states. And forming any entity but continuing to mix personal and business money, which undoes the protection you paid for. All three are avoidable with an hour of planning.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small crossed-out icons. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: an LLC is about liability, not tax. An S corp is about tax, with real costs. A sole proprietorship with clean books is a strong place to start. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes holding a price tag and a calculator. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Why backwards
segments.narration: Why work backwards? Because a rate copied from someone else carries their costs, their hours and their life, not yours. One designer might charge seventy-five an hour with a spouse's health plan and full-time clients. Another charging the same might be losing money once insurance and empty weeks are counted. Your rate has to pay for your life, your taxes and your downtime. So we start from your life and build up to the rate, then check it against the market at the end.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two identical price tags on very different-sized backpacks. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Target
segments.narration: Start with what you want to live on, after tax. Say fifty-five thousand dollars a year.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with a flag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Costs
segments.narration: Add what an employer used to pay for: health insurance, say six thousand a year, retirement, say five thousand, and business costs like software and equipment, say six thousand. If you're not sure about these, look at what you actually spent last year, and remember that an employer's health plan is often worth several hundred dollars a month.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. three small stacks added. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Tax detail
segments.narration: Here's where that eighty-four thousand comes from. On eighty-four thousand of profit, a single filer in twenty twenty-six pays about eleven thousand nine hundred in self-employment tax and about five thousand seven hundred in income tax, after the standard deduction and the twenty percent qualified business income deduction. That's about seventeen thousand six hundred in total, which leaves about sixty-six thousand four hundred. Notice that the tax is about twenty-one percent of profit. That's the number to plan with, not your bracket.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coin stack with a slice taken off the top. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Taxes
segments.narration: Then taxes. Profit has to cover self-employment tax and income tax. Using the twenty twenty-six federal figures for a single filer, about eighty-four thousand of profit leaves roughly sixty-six thousand after federal tax. Enough for the take-home and most of the extras. State tax would add more.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coral slice taken off a tall stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Revenue
segments.narration: So revenue needs to be about ninety thousand: eighty-four thousand profit plus six thousand of business costs. If your business costs are higher, like equipment for a photographer or software for a developer, the revenue target rises one for one.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a tall coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Non-billable
segments.narration: The billable hours step is where most rates go wrong, so let's slow down. A full-time freelancer's week includes finding clients, writing proposals, email, invoicing, bookkeeping, learning, and fixing the computer. That's often ten to twenty hours a week nobody pays for. New freelancers spend even more of their time selling. If you assume thirty-five billable hours a week, you'll set a rate that only works in your best weeks. Track your time for two weeks, honestly, and you'll find your real number.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a clock with part of its face shaded grey. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Time off
segments.narration: And the weeks. Forty-eight working weeks assumes four weeks off for holidays, vacation and sick days combined. No employer is paying for those weeks now. If you want more time off, or you know your work slows down every summer or December, use fewer weeks. Forty-four weeks at twenty-five hours is eleven hundred hours, and the same ninety thousand target becomes about eighty-two dollars an hour.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a calendar with several weeks shaded mint. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Hours
segments.narration: Now the hours. Forty-eight working weeks after holidays and sick days. And you won't bill forty hours a week. Twenty-five is realistic for many freelancers once you count sales, email and admin. That's twelve hundred billable hours.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a clock partly shaded. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Rate
segments.narration: Ninety thousand divided by twelve hundred is seventy-five dollars an hour. That's the floor for this target, not the goal. If you're currently charging fifty, you now know you're working below your target, and by how much. That's not a reason to panic; it's a reason to plan your next rate increase and the clients you'll raise first.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a price tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Packages
segments.narration: Many freelancers do better moving away from hourly altogether. A package, like a brand identity with three logo concepts and two rounds of revisions, lets you charge for the result. As you get faster, you earn more per hour instead of less. Price each package from your hourly floor and an honest hours estimate, then adjust for the value to the client. Put the scope in writing, including what's not included, so extra work becomes a paid change, not a favor.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a neatly wrapped box with a price tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Market check first
segments.narration: Before we go on, a word on the market rate. Look at what experienced people in your niche charge, not what beginners on marketplace sites post. Ask peers directly; many will share ranges. Check job boards for what employers pay salaried staff to do the same work, then remember a freelancer needs well above the equivalent hourly wage to cover the costs we added. If your floor is above what the market pays for your current offer, the answer is usually a sharper niche, not a lower rate.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a row of price tags of different heights. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deposits
segments.narration: Protect your rate from slow payers too. Ask new clients for a deposit, often twenty-five to fifty percent up front for projects. Set payment terms in writing, like fourteen days, and send invoices with a pay-now link. Add a late fee clause if your contract allows it. A client who pays in ninety days is effectively paying you less, because you're covering the gap. Clear terms filter out the clients who were going to be trouble anyway.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. an invoice with a mint check mark and a small clock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Project
segments.narration: If you price by project, convert: estimate the hours honestly, multiply by your rate, and add a margin for revisions.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a project box with a tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Side hustle
segments.narration: A quick second example for side hustlers. Say you have a full-time job in the twenty-two percent bracket and want fifteen thousand dollars extra after tax. Self-employment tax plus income tax on side income at that bracket is roughly thirty percent federal. So you'd need about twenty-one thousand five hundred of profit. At ten hours a week for forty-six weeks, that's four hundred sixty hours, or about forty-seven dollars an hour, before any business costs. Call it fifty. Illustrative, but it shows why side-hustle rates need a tax cushion.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a small briefcase next to a smaller coin stack. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Check
segments.narration: Then sanity-check against the market. If you're far below it, raise your rate. If you're far above, narrow your niche or improve your offer so the price makes sense. And remember the market is wide. The same work is priced very differently for a local shop and for a funded startup, so the client you choose matters as much as the rate you set.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a balance scale. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Raise
segments.narration: Finally, rates aren't set once. Review yours every year, ideally in January. Your costs rise, your skills improve, and your tax bill goes up with your income. Give existing clients notice, usually thirty to sixty days, and a clear new rate. Raise rates for new clients first if you're nervous. And add a minimum project size or a deposit, so small jobs and slow payers don't quietly drag your real hourly rate down.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a price tag being nudged upward on a calendar. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Talk money
segments.narration: Last, how to say your rate. State it plainly, once, with no apology: my rate for this is four thousand five hundred. Then stop talking. If they push back, offer a smaller scope at a lower price rather than the same work for less. Have your floor in mind and be willing to walk away from projects below it. Every client at a rate that doesn't work takes the place of one that does.
segments.on_screen_text: Say it once. Then stop talking.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes standing calmly with a price tag. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: start from take-home pay, add benefits and costs, gross up for tax, divide by billable hours, not total hours. Run these numbers with your own figures this week. It takes twenty minutes with a calculator, and you'll walk into every client conversation knowing exactly where your floor is and why. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.

No text, no logos, no real people.

script.title: Your freelancer tax season plan: January to April
script.hook: Tax season for freelancers isn't one deadline. It's four months with three dates that matter. Here's the plan, week by week, so April is boring. Education, not tax advice. We'll go through January's payment and how to size it, the forms that arrive and the ones you owe, closing the books, finding missed deductions, choosing software or a pro, retirement decisions, what to do if you can't pay, and how to start next year right.

segments.heading: Intro
segments.narration: Tax season for freelancers isn't one deadline. It's four months with three dates that matter. Here's the plan, week by week, so April is boring. Education, not tax advice. We'll go through January's payment and how to size it, the forms that arrive and the ones you owe, closing the books, finding missed deductions, choosing software or a pro, retirement decisions, what to do if you can't pay, and how to start next year right.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes with a four-month calendar strip. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Jan 15
segments.narration: January fifteenth: the last estimated payment for twenty twenty-six. Use the safe harbor or ninety percent of your actual tax. Or file your full return and pay everything by the end of January, and you can skip it.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a January page with a coin. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Which method
segments.narration: To choose your January number quickly: if your income this year was about the same or higher than last year, the safe harbor is usually the smaller payment, a quarter of last year's total tax. If your income dropped, ninety percent of this year's tax spread over the year may be smaller. Our calculator compares both. Either way, after paying, check what's left in your tax savings against your expected April balance, and top it up through February and March if it's short.
segments.on_screen_text: Income up? Safe harbor. Down? Run both.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. two cards, one coral and one mint, on a scale. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Forms
segments.narration: By February first: your 1099-NEC and 1099-K forms arrive. Match every one to your income log. Ask for corrections now, not in April. And if you paid contractors, your own 1099-NECs are due the same day.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a mailbox with forms. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Forms out
segments.narration: Also around February first, the forms you owe. If you paid another freelancer or contractor two thousand dollars or more directly in twenty twenty-six, send them a ten ninety-nine NEC and file it with the IRS by February first. Card and payment-platform payments are reported by the platform, not you. You'll need their W-9, so request it in early January. The IRS has a free online system for filing these forms, and many filing services charge a few dollars per form.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes handing a form to another small mascot. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mismatches
segments.narration: When you match forms to your income log, expect differences. A payment sent in December but received in January belongs to next year for you. A ten ninety-nine K shows gross amounts, before fees. A refund you gave a client might not be reflected. Write a one-line note for each difference. If a form is simply wrong, email the payer with your records and ask for a corrected one. If it doesn't arrive in time, report the right amount and keep your proof.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a ledger and a form with a small connecting line. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: February
segments.narration: February: close the books. Final income total, expenses by category, mileage total, home office measurements, health insurance premiums, retirement contributions. Your tracker or accounting app should give you these in one sitting. Expect it to take one long afternoon if your logs are up to date, or a weekend if they aren't.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a ledger being closed. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Deductions
segments.narration: While closing the books, do one deliberate pass for missed deductions. Payment processor fees, the business share of your phone and internet, software subscriptions, business miles plus parking and tolls, a home office if you qualify, the business part of last year's tax preparation fee, health insurance premiums and HSA contributions. At sixty thousand of profit, every thousand dollars of business expenses you find saves about two hundred thirty dollars of federal tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a magnifying glass over a long receipt. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Software or pro
segments.narration: Then decide who files. Tax software works well for one simple business with clean records. A CPA or enrolled agent is worth it for S corps, several businesses, big purchases, rental property, or an IRS letter. Either way, the business part of the fee is deductible next year. If your income is lower, check whether you qualify for IRS Free File or free volunteer tax help. Book a preparer by February; good ones fill up by March.
segments.on_screen_text: Software vs pro: decide by February
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a fork in a path with two signposts. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: March
segments.narration: March: file, or hand it to your preparer. Filing in March gives you time to fix surprises and get any refund early. Decide on a SEP IRA contribution before you file, because it changes the numbers. If you're due a refund, filing early gets it to you sooner. If you owe, filing early still helps, because you can schedule the payment for April fifteenth and keep the money in savings until then.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a form with a check mark. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Retirement
segments.narration: Before you file, make one retirement decision. If you want to contribute to a SEP IRA for twenty twenty-six, you can open and fund it up to your filing deadline, including extensions, but you need the amount on your return. A traditional IRA contribution for twenty twenty-six, up to seventy-five hundred dollars, or eighty-six hundred if you're fifty or older, can be made until April fifteenth. Either one lowers your income tax. Decide the amount, then file.
segments.on_screen_text: SEP / IRA: decide before you file
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a plant pot with coins as soil. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Balance
segments.narration: If you owe a balance, pay it by April fifteenth, from the tax savings account. If you can't pay it all, file on time anyway and pay what you can. Penalties for not filing are much bigger than for not paying. Check the account balance in March, so there's time to top it up.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a coral vault opening. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Records
segments.narration: While you're in tax mode, decide what to keep. Keep your return, the forms, your income and expense logs, mileage log and receipts for at least three years after you file, longer for anything tied to equipment you're still using. Digital copies are fine. A folder per year, backed up, is enough. If the IRS ever sends a letter asking about something, you'll answer it in minutes.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a row of yearly folders with a small lock. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Extension
segments.narration: An extension to October fifteenth gives you more time to file, not to pay. Estimate and pay what you owe by April fifteenth even if you extend.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a stopwatch with a coin that didn't move. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Can't pay
segments.narration: If your return shows a balance you can't fully pay, file on time anyway and pay as much as you can by April fifteenth. Then set up an IRS payment plan online; for many balances it takes minutes. Interest and a smaller late-payment penalty keep running, so pay it down quickly. What you should never do is skip filing, because the failure-to-file penalty is far bigger. And use the experience to set a higher set-aside percentage for this year.
segments.on_screen_text: Can't pay: file, pay some, payment plan
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a row of small coins stretched across months. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: State
segments.narration: Don't forget your state. If it has an income tax, you'll file a state return and probably owe state estimated payments for the new year too, often on the same dates as the federal ones. Software usually carries your federal numbers over. Check your state's website for its own deadlines, payment portal and any city tax.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a map outline next to a second form. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Q1
segments.narration: Also April fifteenth: your first estimated payment for twenty twenty-seven. Your new safe harbor is this year's total tax. Update your tracker's setup now.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a new calendar page. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Next year
segments.narration: Finally, set up the new year while everything is fresh. Your twenty twenty-six total tax becomes your twenty twenty-seven safe harbor: divide it by four for each quarterly payment if you use that method. Work out your new set-aside percentage from this year's actual tax divided by profit, plus your state. Put the twenty twenty-seven dates in your calendar: April fifteenth, June fifteenth, September fifteenth, and January eighteenth, twenty twenty-eight, because January fifteenth falls on a weekend and the seventeenth is a holiday. Confirm it when the IRS publishes the new form.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. a fresh calendar with four coral dots. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Mindset
segments.narration: One last thing. Tax season feels stressful mostly because of surprises. Every step in this plan exists to move the surprise earlier, to January or February, when you can still do something about it. If you follow it once, next year's version takes half the time, and the year after that, it's routine. That's the goal: boring, predictable, done.
segments.visual_prompt: Clean flat vector illustration, deep navy and warm paper cream with a coral accent and a mint highlight, simple shapes, paper texture. the small paper receipt mascot with a folded corner, round glasses and big eyes relaxing with a cup of tea. No text, no logos, no real people.

segments.heading: Recap
segments.narration: Recap: January fifteenth payment, forms by February first, books closed in February, file in March, pay by April fifteenth, and start the new year's estimates. The Quarterly Tax Tracker in the description handles the logs and the math. Put each of these steps in your calendar now, with a reminder a few days before, so tax season runs on a schedule instead of on stress. Subscribe for one freelancer money move a week.
